title: Opsignal competitive angles vs LLM API providers
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a tactical reference for field reps and solution engineers to use when positioning Redwood Inference against general LLM API providers. Focus is on succinct, repeatable language (soundbites + two-sentence arguments) plus quick counters to typical traps.

Audience / personas to prioritize:
- Platform / infra engineering managers evaluating long-term cost and reliability for product features.
- ML engineering leads concerned about model quality drift and rollouts.
- Security/compliance buyers (SaaS risk, regulated data) who will call out private deployments and auditability.
- Product managers evaluating time-to-market vs operational overhead.

TL;DR soundbites (use-first):
- "If you need predictable SLAs and affordable scale for production LLMs, Redwood treats inference like a first-class service—not just another API."
- "We give you the same API surface across hosted, dedicated, and on‑prem so you can move fast today and lock down later without rewriting integrations."
- "Latency and unit-cost are levers, not unknowns—our observable runtime makes tradeoffs visible and actionable."

Top 4 positioning pillars (reps should memorize):
1) Predictable economics at scale: batching, prefix caching, and quantization controls reduce per-token cost in ways a commodity API cannot guarantee.
2) Operational continuity: canary rollouts, automatic fallbacks, and regional routing keep customer-facing features online during incidents.
3) Deployment flexibility: hosted for speed, reserved Dedicated for predictable throughput, Private for regulated data—one API across all.
4) Production-grade observability: token-level cost/latency traces and regression alerts tied to eval sets.

Competitor comparison (quick grid you can read aloud in 60s)
- Commodity LLM APIs (X, Y): simple, wide model access, good for experimentation. Weaknesses — unpredictable throttling, limited private deployment options, minimal rollout tooling, opaque cost drivers.
- Managed cloud endpoints (A, B): scalable but often tied to a cloud vendor and lacking inference-specific optimizations; limited quantization/batching ergonomics.
- Self-hosted runtimes (open-source stacks): maximum control but significant engineering debt (SRE + ML ops).
- Redwood sweet spot: bridges experimentation → production, reduces ops burden vs self-hosting, gives greater reliability and cost controls than commodity APIs.

Common sales traps and suggested rebuttals (short and long forms)
Trap: "We're fine just calling the big public API — cheaper and faster to integrate."
- Short: "Public APIs hide unit economics that explode at scale. We make those costs visible and controllable."
- Long: "Early integration looks cheaper because it ignores throttling, caching inefficiencies, and the operational effort to handle degraded responses. We provide batching, cache layers, and rollouts that reduce both token spend and incident toil. For teams with predictable traffic, customers often see 20–40% lower per-token costs within a month."

Trap: "We don't need private deployment — our data isn't sensitive."
- Short: "Private is as much about control and auditability as it is about sensitive data."
- Long: "Even non-sensitive payloads may require region residency, audit trails, or certs for compliance or procurement. Private deployments also let you pin ML versions and control upgrade windows—important for deterministic product behavior."

Trap: "We'll self-host, it's cheaper long-term."
- Short: "Self-hosting transfers hidden costs from vendor to your team."
- Long: "Self-hosting requires ongoing investment: kernel tuning, performance regressions, incident ops, and model onboarding. Most teams underestimate that maintenance costs can exceed vendor fees and slow product iterations. For regulated workloads or extreme customization, self-hosting makes sense — otherwise Redwood often has a lower total cost of ownership."

Objection scripts (role-play ready, 30–60s)
- Security/Compliance: "What about logs and keys?"
  Response: "We integrate with KMS/HSM and provide audit logs and a private control plane for Private deployments. If you require an air-gapped install, we have a tested on-prem package and professional services to reduce lift."

- SRE/Infra: "How do you handle traffic spikes and throttling?"
  Response: "Our Dedicated pools support predictable throughput with autoscaling and burst policies. We also support region-based routing and automatic fallback to compatible variants to prevent failed requests from hitting your app."

- ML Lead: "How do you prevent regressions when we change models?"
  Response: "We tie quality monitoring to eval sets and can alert on regression thresholds. Rollouts are first-class: canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to earlier versions if quality or latency degrades."

Tactical demo scripts and quick wins to show live (SRE + SE pairing)
1) Latency/sla demo: Deploy two routes—one on Hosted and one on Dedicated with same model. Run a synthetic burst and show token-level latency and cost breakdown in Console. Call out fallback in action.
2) Cost delta demo: Present a real example where caching + batching reduces token spend on a common prompt pattern. Show before/after token counts and unit costs.
3) Rollout fail-safe: Start a canary with slightly different model weights; intentionally inject a prompt set that triggers regressions and show automatic rollback.

Do-not-say list (avoid absolute promises or technical inaccuracies)
- "We will always be cheaper" — inaccurate. Use "more controllable economics" instead.
- "We support every open model out of the box" — avoid unless verified for the specific model.
- Absolute latency guarantees without SLA context — reference our SLA tiers.

Data points and anecdotes to memorize (use sparingly, tag with source)
- Typical Hosted → Dedicated customers see 15–35% reduction in per-token spend after moving predictable workloads. (internal: GT-1423)
- Incident anecdote: Customer X moved to Dedicated and avoided outage by using regional fallback during a cloud provider maintenance window (see case note: confluence:incident-2024-06-19).

Collateral checklist (priorities for field kit)
- One-page cost explainer (calculator example) — must include batching/cache effects.
- Demo scripts (SRE/SE playbook) — step-by-step with expected Console screenshots.
- Short checklist for security reviewers — KMS/HSM, audit logs, network diagrams.
- Quick migration guide from public APIs — code snippets for switching an endpoint with minimal changes.

Open questions and follow-ups (owner: Marco Li)
- Can we get two anonymized customer cost baselines (Hosted vs Dedicated) for GT materials? (jira:GT-1423)
- Draft a 1-page private-deployment security checklist tailored for regulated customers. (confluence:security-private-deploy-template)
- Record a 6-minute demo video showing cost delta and rollback — script to be finalized.

Next actions (this week)
- SEs: test demo 1 in sandbox and confirm screenshots (Evelyn).
- Content: produce the one-page cost explainer draft (Aisha).
- Legal/security: validate wording for KMS/HSM claims (Diego).

Notes to self: keep the language low-friction for PMs — they want predictable timelines and examples of "what breaks if we don't control upgrades." For execs, emphasize risk reduction and predictable economics.
